name: Brentford & Isleworth Meeting House
text: Your train passes near the Quaker meeting house in Isleworth, on the train's {side}, built in 1785 on land bought for £35. It is one of the oldest purpose-built meeting houses in London, with a Quaker burial ground and a garden around it.

name: The Pines, Putney
text: Your train passes near The Pines, on the train's {side}, a house on Putney Hill where the poet Algernon Charles Swinburne lived with his friend Theodore Watts-Dunton until his death in 1909. Max Beerbohm, who often visited, described it as 'but a few steps from the railway-station'.

name: Surrey Iron Railway
text: Your train passes near where the Surrey Iron Railway began, on the train's {side}, at a dock on the Thames at Wandsworth. From 1803 its horse-drawn wagons carried coal, lime and building materials about nine miles to Croydon, until it closed in 1846.

name: The Falcon, Battersea
text: Your train passes near the Falcon, on the train's {side}, a pub on St John's Hill recorded as an inn in 1733; the present building dates from 1882 to 1883. The Campaign for Real Ale describes its curved bar counter as the longest in Britain.

name: Wandsworth Common Windmill
text: Your train passes Wandsworth Common Windmill, on the train's {side}, a small smock mill built in 1837 to drain water from this railway's cutting. It pumped the water into an ornamental lake on the common called the Black Sea, and stopped work after the lake was filled in around 1884.

name: Wimbledon Traincare Depot
text: Your train passes Wimbledon Traincare Depot, on the train's {side}, where South Western Railway's trains are looked after. Opened in 1974, it is one of the busiest depots in the country, with about 250 carriages maintained here each night.

name: New Wimbledon Theatre
text: Your train passes near the New Wimbledon Theatre, on the train's {side}, an Edwardian theatre that opened on Boxing Day 1910 with the pantomime Jack and Jill. Lionel Bart's Oliver! had its world premiere here in 1960, and it seems to have been the only British theatre with a Turkish bath in the basement.

name: New Malden War Memorial
text: Your train passes near New Malden's war memorial, on the train's {side}, a three-tiered cenotaph in the High Street unveiled in 1924 by a soldier who had been blinded in the First World War. It was slightly damaged in 1940 when a bomb fell close by during the Blitz.

name: Kingsmeadow
text: Your train passes near Kingsmeadow, on the train's {side}, a football ground built by Kingstonian in 1989. AFC Wimbledon played here from 2002 until 2020, and it is now the home ground of Chelsea Women.

name: Lovekyn Chapel
text: Your train passes near the Lovekyn Chapel, on the train's {side}, founded by Edward Lovekyn in 1309, with later gifts from his son John and from William Walworth. It is still used by Kingston Grammar School, whose roots go back to at least the 13th century.

name: Kingston Railway Bridge
text: Your train crosses the Thames on Kingston Railway Bridge, built in 1907 to replace a cast-iron bridge of 1863. Three of its five arches span the river, and the other two are over dry land.

name: Normansfield Hospital
text: Your train passes near Normansfield, on the train's {side}, opened in 1868 by Dr John Langdon Down, after whom Down syndrome is named, as a home for children with learning disabilities. Its Victorian theatre opened in 1879, and the building now houses the Langdon Down Museum of Learning Disability.

name: New Malden High Street
text: Your train passes near New Malden High Street, on the train's {side}, known for its many Korean shops and restaurants: New Malden has the largest community of South Koreans in Europe.

name: Surbiton station
text: Surbiton station, at one end of this stretch, was rebuilt in 1937 in an Art Deco style designed by James Robb Scott, and has been called one of the finest modernist stations in Britain. It appears in the very first episode of ITV's Agatha Christie's Poirot.

name: Raynes Park station
text: Raynes Park station, at one end of this stretch, opened in 1871. Its platforms aren't opposite each other, so its long footbridge crosses the four main-line tracks at an angle.

name: Malden Manor
text: Your train passes near the manor house of Malden, on the train's {side}, beside St John's church and mentioned in the Domesday Book. In 1264 Walter de Merton founded a college here, which later moved to Oxford as Merton College.

name: Tolworth Tower
text: Your train passes near Tolworth Tower, on the train's {side}, a 22-storey office block 81 metres high beside the Kingston bypass, opened in 1964. The supermarket on its ground floor, first a Fine Fare, was the largest in England when it opened.

name: Corinthian-Casuals F.C.
text: Your train passes near the ground of Corinthian-Casuals, on the train's {side}, an amateur club formed in 1939 by joining Corinthian, founded in 1882, with Casuals. On a tour of Brazil in the 1988 to 1989 season they played Corinthians, and Sócrates turned out for both teams.

name: St Mary the Virgin's Church, Chessington
text: Your train passes near St Mary the Virgin's Church in Chessington, on the train's {side}, whose chancel dates from the 12th century; a chapel here is mentioned in Merton Priory's records from 1174 to 1189. When the plaster ceiling was taken down in its Victorian restoration, the date 1636 was found and the old chestnut roof revealed.

name: Sir Joseph Hood Memorial Wood
text: Your train passes near Sir Joseph Hood Memorial Wood, on the train's {side}, a small nature reserve of oaks planted in the middle of the 19th century, probably as cover for hunting. It is named after Sir Joseph Hood, a former MP and Mayor of Wimbledon.

name: Elm Grove tube station
text: Your train passes the site of Elm Grove, on the train's {side}, a station also called Tennis Ground that was planned beside the All England Lawn Tennis and Croquet Club's original grounds, for a line approved in 1910 on which the District Railway was to run trains. In the end the Southern Railway built this line, and the station was never built.

name: Rutlish School
text: Your train passes near Rutlish School, on the train's {side}, named after William Rutlish, embroiderer to Charles II, who left £400 when he died in 1687 to educate poor children of the parish. John Major, Prime Minister from 1990 to 1997, was a pupil at the school.

name: Baitul Futuh Mosque
text: Your train passes Baitul Futuh, on the train's {side}, one of the largest mosque complexes in Europe, completed in 2003 for the Ahmadiyya Muslim Community. Paid for entirely by donations, it can hold 13,000 worshippers.

name: St Lawrence Church, Morden
text: Your train passes near St Lawrence Church, on the train's {side}, Morden's parish church, built in 1636 at the highest point of Morden, overlooking Morden Park. It is listed at Grade I.

name: Pyl Brook
text: Your train passes near the Pyl Brook, on the train's {side}, a small stream that rises in Sutton Common and flows through Merton to join the Beverley Brook in New Malden. Its name probably comes from the Old English pyll, a pool or small stream.

name: Gander Green Lane
text: Your train passes Gander Green Lane, on the train's {side}, the home ground of Sutton United. On January 7th 1989 Sutton beat Coventry City, then in the top division, by two goals to one here, one of the biggest upsets in FA Cup history.

name: The Messenger (David Wynne sculpture)
text: Your train passes The Messenger, on the train's {side}, a life-size bronze by David Wynne of a horse and a young rider, put up beside Sutton station in 1981. The rider raises one hand as if calling out, and the horse looks towards the station.

name: Whitehall, Cheam
text: Your train passes near Whitehall, on the train's {side}, a timber-framed house in Cheam village thought to have been built around 1500 as a yeoman farmer's house. It is now a museum, with a room about Henry VIII's nearby Nonsuch Palace.

name: Belmont Pastures
text: Your train passes Belmont Pastures, on the train's {side}, a narrow strip of old meadow beside the line that once belonged to Belmont Hospital. Now a nature reserve, its chalk grassland has wild flowers such as bladder campion and knapweed, and grasshoppers and crickets.

name: Carshalton House
text: Your train passes near Carshalton House, on the train's {side}, built around 1710 for a tobacco merchant who went bankrupt a few years later. In its grounds a water tower of about 1721 pumped water to the house and fountains, and has a bathroom still lined with Delft tiles; the house is now St Philomena's School.

name: The Cock sign
text: Your train passes near the Cock sign, on the train's {side}, which stands over a crossroads in Sutton High Street. It was put up in 1907 as the sign of the Cock Hotel, later became a road sign and lamp post, and was listed in 2018.

name: Carshalton Park
text: Your train passes near Carshalton Park, on the train's {side}, now about a tenth of its original size, as the rest was sold for housing from 1892. There were deer in the park until 1898.

name: Waddon Ponds
text: Your train passes near Waddon Ponds, on the train's {side}, one of the sources of the River Wandle and one of very few places in Croydon where the river can be seen above ground.

name: Croydon Palace
text: Your train passes near Croydon Palace, on the train's {side}, the summer residence of the Archbishops of Canterbury for more than 500 years, where Henry III and Elizabeth I were regular visitors. From 1889 to 2025 it was a girls' school.

name: Croydon Common Athletic Ground
text: Your train passes the site of the Nest, on the train's {side}, home ground of Croydon Common from 1908 to 1917 and of Crystal Palace from 1918 to 1924. A train depot now stands on the site, and the ground's front wall still stands along Selhurst Road.

name: BRIT School
text: Your train passes near the BRIT School, on the train's {side}, a school for the performing and creative arts, free to attend, that opened in 1991. Adele and Amy Winehouse are among its former pupils.

name: J. W. Hobbs' Ground
text: Your train passes near the site of J. W. Hobbs' Ground, on the train's {side}, a cricket ground laid out in 1885 in the grounds of Norbury Hall. Its only first-class match was against the touring Australians in 1888, and cricket went on here until a leisure centre was built on it in the 1990s.

name: Norbury Estate
text: Your train passes near the Norbury Estate, on the train's {side}, a London County Council cottage estate built from 1901 to 1920 and influenced by the garden city movement. It stands on an old brickfield, whose clay was fired to make bricks for the estate.

name: Tooting Bec Lido
text: Your train passes Tooting Bec Lido, on the train's {side}, opened in 1906 and the largest freshwater swimming pool by surface area in the UK, 100 yards long and 33 yards wide. Brad Pitt's pool scene in the film Snatch was shot here.

name: Chez Bruce
text: Your train passes near Chez Bruce, on the train's {side}, a restaurant opened in 1995 that has held a Michelin star since 1999. It is on the site of Harveys, Marco Pierre White's former restaurant.
